kurals.tamil:
செல்லாமை உண்டேல் எனக்குரை மற்றுநின்
வல்வரவு வாழ்வார்க் குரை.
kurals.transliteration:
Sellaamai undael enakkurai matrunin
valvaravu vaazhvaark kurai.
kurals.meaning: If you are not going to leave, tell me so; but if your news is that you will go and hurry back, tell it to whoever will still be alive when you return.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your best friend says, ‘I’m moving away, but don’t worry, I’ll visit soon!’ You might answer, ‘Only tell me the part where you’re staying. The coming-back-soon part is too far away for me to hold on to.’ The wife in this couplet feels the same: a promise to return quickly is no comfort if her heart cannot last that long.
kurals.university: Chapter 116 opens the karpiyal (the section on married love) with the heroine’s distress when her husband announces a journey, conventionally to earn wealth or serve the king; commentators assign the couplets to the heroine herself or to her confidante (tōḻi) speaking for her. Cellāmai (செல்லாமை) is ‘not going’, and valvaravu (வல்வரவு) is ‘swift return’; the sting is in vāḻvārkku urai, ‘tell it to those who will live’, implying that she will not survive the interval. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘tell it to those able to stay alive until then’, while Kalaignar turns it into ‘say your farewells now to whoever will still be alive when you come back’. Pope renders: ‘If you will say, “I leave thee not,” then tell me so; / Of quick return tell those that can survive this woe.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Rama tells Sita he must go into forest exile and that she should stay behind in Ayodhya, she refuses, insisting that a wife’s place is at her husband’s side and that the forest with him is better than a palace without him.
hinduism.explanation: In the Ayodhya Kanda, Sita answers Rama’s farewell by declaring she will go with him, since separation from him would be worse than any hardship of the forest.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Sita will not accept a parting softened by assurances; for her there are only two options, staying together or not surviving the absence.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda, Sita’s plea to accompany Rama (sargas c. 27-30) (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; a strong situational match, though Sita succeeds in going while the Kural’s heroine can only protest.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And they all wept sore, and fell on Paul’s neck, and kissed him, Sorrowing most of all for the words which he spake, that they should see his face no more.”
christianity.explanation: When Paul announces his departure from Miletus, the elders of Ephesus are grieved above all by his words that they will not see him again.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, it is the announcement of the parting, the words themselves, that wounds most deeply.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; captures grief at a spoken farewell, but the bond is pastoral rather than marital and Paul does not promise to return.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Abraham! Where are you going, leaving us in this valley where there is no person whose company we may enjoy, nor is there anything (to enjoy)?”
islam.explanation: Hagar follows Abraham as he leaves her and the infant Ishmael in the empty valley of Mecca, repeating her question until she learns that God has commanded it.
islam.tie_back: Hagar, like the Kural’s heroine, confronts a departing husband with the question of how she is to survive his absence.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a close situational parallel, though Hagar ends by trusting God where the Kural’s heroine ends in bitter irony.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Entreat me not to leave thee, and to return from following after thee; for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge.”
judaism.explanation: Ruth refuses Naomi’s urging to turn back, binding herself to go wherever Naomi goes until death parts them.
judaism.tie_back: Ruth voices the Kural’s refusal of separation as a vow: the only acceptable answer to a parting is not to part.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); the refusal to be parted matches, but the bond is between in-laws, not spouses.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Lord, as I was leaving home, a Sakyan girl — the envy of the countryside — glanced up at me, with her hair half-combed, and said, ‘Hurry back, master.’”
buddhism.explanation: Nanda, the Buddha’s half-brother, confesses that the parting words of his bride keep pulling him back from the monastic life.
buddhism.tie_back: The bride’s ‘Hurry back’ is the very plea for a swift return that the Kural’s heroine says she cannot live on.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a genuine scene of a bride’s parting plea, though the sutta’s point is Nanda’s eventual freedom from that attachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Râgîmatî thought: ‘Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.’”
jainism.explanation: When her betrothed, Arishtanemi, leaves on the wedding day to become a monk, Princess Rajimati feels her life as she knew it has ended and resolves to renounce the world herself.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati, like the Kural’s heroine, treats her beloved’s departure as the end of the life she had; the Jain story turns that ending into renunciation.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi’s diacritics simplified); a genuine Jain story of a woman forsaken by a departing groom, though its resolution is religious rather than romantic.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s Heroides, Laodamia writes to her husband Protesilaus, who sailed for Troy almost at once after their wedding, that she fainted as his ship left and begs him to come home to her quickly and safely.
greek_mythology.explanation: Laodamia’s letter is a whole poem of a newly married wife unable to bear her husband’s departure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She, too, receives a hasty departure and a hoped-for return, and finds the gap between them almost unendurable.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s situation, not checked against a translation this session; a strong parallel in a wife’s distress at a husband’s journey.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that just as lovers find the sight of the beloved the most delightful thing, so friends find nothing more desirable than living together.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, shared presence is not an extra but the very activity in which love and friendship consist.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same: the only news she wants is that he will stay.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it states the value of presence but not the threat of a parting.

kurals.tamil:
இன்கண் உடைத்தவர் பார்வல் பிரிவஞ்சும்
புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு.
kurals.transliteration:
Inkan udaiththavar paarval pirivanjum
punkan udaiththaal punarvu.
kurals.meaning: Once, even his look was pure delight; now even our embrace is filled with pain, because I dread the parting that is coming.
kurals.elementary: Think of the last day of a wonderful holiday. You are still at the beach, the sun is shining, but you keep thinking, ‘Tomorrow we go home,’ and the fun feels a little sad. The wife in this couplet feels that way: her husband is still with her, but knowing he will leave makes even being close to him hurt.
kurals.university: The couplet contrasts the past and present of the same relationship: avar pārval (அவர் பார்வல், ‘his look’) once had iṉkaṇ (இன்கண், ‘sweetness, joy’), but now even puṇarvu (புணர்வு, ‘union, being together’) has puṉkaṇ (புன்கண், ‘distress’) because of pirivu añcum, ‘fearing separation’. The two rhyming nouns iṉkaṇ and puṉkaṇ carry the turn from joy to grief. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read pārval as his loving look, while Solomon Pappaiah contrasts his pleasing look with his conduct, which signals that he is about to leave; Kalaignar sharpens the contrast between gazing and embracing. Pope: ‘It once was perfect joy to look upon his face; / But now the fear of parting saddens each embrace.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gopi Gita, the cowherd women tell Krishna that when he goes off to the forest by day, a single moment without seeing him feels like an age to them.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana makes the gopis’ longing for the sight of Krishna the model of devotion, and their pain in his absence its measure.
hinduism.tie_back: The gopis share the Kural’s sense that the sight of the beloved is pure joy, and that the shadow of his going spoils it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; it matches the joy of seeing and the pain of absence, but not the dread that poisons an embrace while he is still present.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother’s house.”
christianity.explanation: The bride in the Song of Songs, having found her beloved after searching for him, clings to him for fear of losing him again.
christianity.tie_back: Her clinging embrace is shaped by the same fear of loss that, in the Kural, turns being together into anxiety.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; shows an embrace shaped by fear of losing the beloved, though the Song’s mood here is triumphant rather than sorrowful.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Jacob] said, ‘Indeed, it saddens me that you should take him, and I fear that a wolf would eat him while you are of him unaware.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob is grieved by the mere proposal that Joseph leave his side, even for a day.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Jacob is pained in advance; the loved one is still present, but the coming separation already hurts.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a good match for grief that comes before the parting, though between father and son rather than lovers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another.”
judaism.explanation: Laban and Jacob name the cairn Mizpah as they part, asking God to keep watch over the bond while they are apart.
judaism.tie_back: The Mizpah words show a meeting already shaped by the coming absence, which is the mood of the Kural’s embrace.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); later used as a lovers’ farewell, but in context it is a wary pact between rivals, so the fit is loose.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that the same affection that delights us is the root of the grief and fear of losing what we love.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural describes this exact process: the joy of his presence has become the fear of his absence.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it diagnoses the same turn from endearment to fear, though it recommends letting go where the Kural only laments.

jainism.quote_or_event: “All singing is but prattle, all dancing is but mocking, all ornaments are but a burden, all pleasures produce but pains.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citra warns his former brother, King Brahmadatta, that every pleasure carries the seed of its own suffering.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds out the same thing in her own life: the delight of union has already turned into pain.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the doctrine that pleasure turns to pain fits, but it is general renunciant teaching, not about love or parting.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orpheus is allowed to lead Eurydice back from the underworld on condition he does not look at her until they reach the light; near the end, afraid of losing her, he turns to look, and she slips away from him a second time.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s telling, it is Orpheus’s anxious love and fear of losing her that make him look back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved’s presence and the lover’s look are spoiled by dread of separation.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; shares the theme of a loving look shadowed by fear of loss, but the circumstances are mythic rather than domestic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises that when you kiss your child or your wife, you should remind yourself that you are kissing a human being, so that if they are taken from you, you will not be disturbed.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic exercise deliberately brings the thought of separation into moments of affection, in order to free the mind from dread.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has the same thought of parting in the middle of an embrace, but in her it brings only pain, which is exactly the disturbance Epictetus hopes to remove.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; the same situation, approached with the opposite attitude.

kurals.tamil:
அரிதரோ தேற்றம் அறிவுடையார் கண்ணும்
பிரிவோ ரிடத்துண்மை யான்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aridharo thaetram arivudaiyaar kannum
pirivo ritaththunmai yaan.
kurals.meaning: Since parting happens at some time even with a wise and understanding lover, it is hard to feel sure of anyone’s promise never to leave.
kurals.elementary: Suppose the kindest, smartest grown-up you know promises, ‘I’ll always be here.’ Then one day they have to go away for work. Next time someone promises you that, it is harder to believe, even if they mean it. The wife in this couplet feels the same: if even a wise, loving husband sometimes leaves, how can she trust any promise to stay?
kurals.university: Tēṟṟam (தேற்றம்) means ‘certainty, confidence’ and arito (அரிதரோ, with the emphatic particle aro) ‘is indeed hard’. Aṟivuṭaiyār kaṇṇum (அறிவுடையார் கண்ணும்), ‘even in those who have understanding’, refers to the husband, who knows how much his absence will hurt; pirivu ōr iṭattu uṇmaiyāṉ (பிரிவு ஓர் இடத்து உண்மையான்), ‘since separation exists at one time or another’, gives the reason. The printed form pirivō riṭattuṇmai is a sandhi run-together of pirivu ōr iṭattu uṇmai, and editions agree on the wording. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan take tēṟṟam to be her confidence in his ‘I will not leave’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as her inability to be sure of his love. Pope: ‘To trust henceforth is hard, if ever he depart, / E’en he, who knows his promise and my breaking heart.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: Nala, a king famed for virtue who had won Damayanti and sworn devotion to her, abandons her while she sleeps in the forest after he loses his kingdom at dice.
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata’s Nala episode, even a good and wise husband, under the pressure of misfortune, leaves the wife who trusted him.
hinduism.tie_back: Nala is a clear example of the Kural’s fear: even an understanding husband may, at some point, part from his wife.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; a strong parallel, though Nala acts under a curse and in despair rather than for wealth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Peter said unto him, Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee. Likewise also said all the disciples.”
christianity.explanation: Peter and the other disciples sincerely swear never to forsake Jesus, and within hours they scatter and deny him.
christianity.tie_back: As the Kural warns, even sincere and understanding people break their ‘I will never leave’, which makes such promises hard to rely on.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a good example of a sincere vow not to part being broken, though the bond is discipleship, not marriage.

islam.quote_or_event: “Everyone upon it [i.e., the earth] will perish, And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that every created being passes away and only God endures.
islam.tie_back: If everything on earth is subject to passing, then, as the Kural concludes, no human promise of permanent presence can be fully trusted.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (footnote marker removed); it supports the general truth that separation is universal but is about mortality, not lovers’ promises.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah teaches that any love that depends on some particular thing ceases when that thing ceases, while love that does not depend on anything never ceases; it contrasts Amnon’s love for Tamar with the love of David and Jonathan.
judaism.explanation: Pirkei Avot distinguishes love that will not last from love that does, and suggests that it is hard to know from outside which is which.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine faces the same uncertainty: she cannot be sure whether her husband’s love will outlast the reasons that now call him away.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known mishnah (numbered 5:16 or 5:19 in different editions), not checked this session; it speaks to how lasting love is rather than to physical separation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘I will grow different, separate from all that is dear and appealing to me.’”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists separation from all that is dear among five facts that every person, lay or ordained, should reflect on often.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s premise stated as doctrine: separation comes to everyone, the wise included, so no promise can rule it out.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.57, Upajjhatthana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a close match to the Kural’s claim that separation is unavoidable, though the sutta draws a lesson of non-attachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Time elapses and quickly pass the days; the pleasures of men are not permanent; they come to a man and leave him just as a bird leaves a tree void of fruit.”
jainism.explanation: King Brahmadatta admits to the monk Citra that worldly joys come and go and cannot be held on to.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has learned the same thing about love: what comes to us also leaves, so no promise of permanence is certain.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the impermanence of joys fits well, though the verse speaks of pleasures in general, not of a beloved.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Abandoned by Theseus on the island of Naxos after he had sworn to marry her, Ariadne laments that from now on no woman should believe a man’s oath or trust that his words are faithful.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Catullus’s retelling, Ariadne draws a general lesson about trust from one desertion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She reaches the Kural’s conclusion: once even a trusted lover has left, confidence in any promise becomes hard.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage, not checked against a translation this session; the logic is very close, though Theseus is faithless while the Kural’s husband is not.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that friendships based on pleasure or usefulness are easily dissolved, because when the pleasure or use ends, so does the bond.
philosophy.explanation: Only friendship of character, he argues, is lasting; others depend on changing circumstances.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has reason to doubt because circumstances, such as the need to earn, can pull even a loving partner away.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; it explains why bonds dissolve, but the Kural’s husband leaves for duty, not because his love has failed.

kurals.tamil:
அளித்தஞ்சல் என்றவர் நீப்பின் தெளித்தசொல்
தேறியார்க்கு உண்டோ தவறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Aliththanjal endravar neeppin theliththasol
thaeriyaarkku undo thavaru.
kurals.meaning: If the one who lovingly said ‘Do not be afraid’ goes away, is it the fault of the one who believed his reassuring words?
kurals.elementary: Imagine a parent says, ‘Don’t worry, I’ll be right here,’ and then leaves the room. Would it be your fault for believing them? Of course not. The wife in this couplet asks the same question: her husband promised she need not fear, so how can she be blamed for trusting him?
kurals.university: Aḷittu (அளித்து) is ‘having shown grace, having loved’ and añcal (அஞ்சல்) is the prohibitive ‘do not fear’; together they recall the husband’s reassurance at the start of their life together, which Solomon Pappaiah places at the time of marriage. Nīppiṉ (நீப்பின்) is ‘if he leaves’, and teḷitta col tēṟiyārkku (தெளித்த சொல் தேறியார்க்கு) ‘to those who trusted the words that made them clear (free of doubt)’. The question uṇṭō tavaṟu (உண்டோ தவறு, ‘is there any fault?’) is rhetorical: the fault lies with the one who promised. Commentators agree on this reading; Pope: ‘If he depart, who fondly said, “Fear not,” what blame’s incurred / By those who trusted to his reassuring word?’

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Dushyanta marries Shakuntala in the hermitage, gives her his signet ring and promises to send for her, but when she later comes to his court he does not recognise her and rejects her.
hinduism.explanation: In Kalidasa’s play, Shakuntala is publicly shamed for having trusted the king’s word, though the fault lies with his forgetting (caused by a curse).
hinduism.tie_back: Shakuntala’s position is the Kural’s question acted out: is the one who trusted a lover’s promise to blame when he fails her?
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known plot, not checked against a translation this session; a strong parallel of a broken reassurance, though the play blames a curse rather than the husband.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.”
christianity.explanation: On the night before he leaves them, Jesus tells his disciples not to be afraid, and he promises to come again to them.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus’ ‘neither let it be afraid’ answers to the Kural’s añcal (‘fear not’); where the Kural fears a reassurance broken, the Gospel presents one meant to be kept.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a ‘do not be afraid’ spoken on the eve of departure, though offered as a trustworthy promise rather than one in doubt.

islam.quote_or_event: “So We restored him to his mother that she might be content and not grieve and that she would know that the promise of Allah is true.”
islam.explanation: Moses’ mother sets her baby adrift on God’s assurance that he will be returned to her, and the Qur’an stresses that the promise was kept.
islam.tie_back: The verse contrasts with the Kural: God’s ‘do not fear’ proves true, while the human lover’s reassurance is what the heroine fears will be broken.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a contrast of a divine reassurance kept against a human one in doubt, not a direct parallel.

judaism.quote_or_event: In Hosea, God promises to betroth Israel to Himself forever, in righteousness, justice, lovingkindness, compassion and faithfulness, so that the bride may trust that this time she will not be abandoned.
judaism.explanation: The prophet uses the language of marriage to describe a faithfulness that does not break its word.
judaism.tie_back: Hosea offers the kind of promise the Kural’s heroine longs to trust, and shows by contrast how much hurt a broken ‘fear not’ can do.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against JPS this session; a contrast of faithful betrothal rather than a parallel to broken reassurance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In Ashvaghosha’s life of the Buddha, Yashodhara, waking to find that Siddhartha has left the palace in the night, laments that he abandoned her while she slept and did not take her with him as ancient kings took their wives into the forest.
buddhism.explanation: Yashodhara’s grief is sharpened by the sense that she trusted a husband who then left without warning.
buddhism.tie_back: She asks, in effect, the Kural’s question: what fault was it of mine, who trusted him, that he should go?
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known lament, not checked against a translation this session; a close emotional parallel, though Buddhist tradition presents the departure as necessary for liberation.

jainism.quote_or_event: Princess Rajimati is promised in marriage to Arishtanemi, but on the wedding day, seeing animals penned for the feast, he gives away his ornaments and leaves to become a monk; she is left overwhelmed with grief.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana tells how a betrothal everyone trusted ended on the wedding day itself.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati, who trusted the match, is left in the Kural’s position, though the Jain text treats the groom’s departure as an act of compassion rather than a broken promise.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a narrative read on sacred-texts.com this session; strong situational overlap, but Jainism honours the groom’s leaving, which reverses the Kural’s judgement.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Dido learns that Aeneas is secretly preparing his fleet to leave Carthage, she confronts him, reproaching him for hoping to slip away in silence and appealing to the pledges and union they had shared.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Virgil, Dido treats Aeneas’s departure as a betrayal of everything she had believed from him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Dido’s anguish asks the Kural’s question: is the one who trusted to blame when the lover leaves?
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene, not checked against a translation this session; a close parallel, though Aeneas never formally married Dido.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant argues that making a promise one does not intend to keep cannot be made a universal law, because if everyone did it, no one would believe a promise at all.
philosophy.explanation: For Kant, promising depends on trust, and breaking one’s word harms the very practice of promising.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows the cost on a small scale: a broken ‘fear not’ damages her ability to trust any promise.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, section II (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known argument; it concerns deliberately false promises, while the Kural’s husband may have meant his words.

kurals.tamil:
ஓம்பின் அமைந்தார் பிரிவோம்பல் மற்றவர்
நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ompin amaindhaar pirivompal matravar
neengin aridhaal punarvu.
kurals.meaning: If you want to save me, keep my husband from going; for once he has left, being together again will be hard to come by.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever seen a balloon start to float away? It is much easier to hold the string tight before it leaves your hand than to catch the balloon once it is in the sky. The wife in this couplet says the same: stop him from leaving now, because once he is gone, getting him back will be very hard.
kurals.university: Ompiṉ (ஓம்பின்) is ‘if you would protect (me)’, and amaintār (அமைந்தார்) ‘the one who is fitted (to me)’, that is, her destined husband; pirivu ōmpal (பிரிவு ஓம்பல்) means ‘prevent the parting’. The warning follows: avar nīṅkiṉ arito puṇarvu (அவர் நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு), ‘if he leaves, union is hard’, with the commentarial suggestion that she may not live to see his return. Commentators take the couplet as the heroine’s words to her confidante, asking her to stop the departure; Solomon Pappaiah instead has the husband himself, as the one whose role is to protect her life, avoid leaving her. Pope: ‘If you would guard my life, from going him restrain / Who fills my life! If he depart, hardly we meet again.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Akrura arrives to take Krishna and Balarama to Mathura, the gopis of Vraja lament, blame the ‘cruel’ Akrura and fate, and cling around the chariot in an attempt to keep Krishna from going.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana describes the gopis’ desperate attempt to prevent the separation they fear will be permanent.
hinduism.tie_back: The gopis do what the Kural’s heroine asks of her friend: they try to stop the departure, sure that reunion afterwards will be hard.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; a close parallel, and their fear proved right, since Krishna did not return to Vraja.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them.”
christianity.explanation: On the road to Emmaus, the two disciples urge the stranger, who is the risen Jesus, not to go on but to stay with them.
christianity.tie_back: Their plea ‘Abide with us’ is the action the Kural asks for: keep the beloved from going before the chance is lost.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the plea to stay matches, though the setting is hospitality, not a lover’s departure.

islam.quote_or_event: “The date-palm cried like a child! The Prophet (ﷺ) descended (the pulpit) and embraced it while it continued moaning like a child being quietened.”
islam.explanation: When the Prophet stopped preaching beside the palm trunk and moved to a new pulpit, the trunk wept until he came back and held it.
islam.tie_back: The weeping trunk shows the Kural’s grief at the loved one’s moving away, a grief that only his return could quiet.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 3584 (Book of Virtues and Merits)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a moving image of grief at separation from a beloved presence, though it is a miracle narrative, not a story of lovers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; But my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: The woman in the Song of Songs hesitates for a moment, and when she opens the door her beloved has gone; she then searches for him in vain.
judaism.tie_back: Her search illustrates the Kural’s warning: once the beloved has left, finding him again is hard.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); shows how hard reunion is once the beloved has gone, though there it follows her delay, not his planned journey.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Therefore hold nothing dear, for separation from the dear is painful. There are no bonds for those who have nothing beloved or unloved.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that because parting from the beloved is painful, one should not cling to anything as dear.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural tries to prevent the painful parting; the Dhammapada prevents the pain at its root by releasing the attachment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; same diagnosis of the pain of parting, opposite remedy.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Now, as this sacred tree Manôrama is shaken by the storm, the birds, suffering, destitute of refuge, and miserable, scream aloud.”
jainism.explanation: When King Nami leaves Mithila to become a monk and the city is in uproar, he compares his people to birds crying when the tree that sheltered them is shaken.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine fears becoming one of those birds, left without shelter when the one she depends on goes.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a vivid image of those left behind by a departure, though Nami’s leaving is presented as admirable renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Andromache meets Hector at the Scaean gate and begs him to stay on the walls and not go out to fight, warning that if he goes she will be left a widow and their son an orphan.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Iliad, Andromache tries to prevent a departure she fears will be final.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She makes the Kural’s plea directly: keep him from going, because once he is gone there may be no meeting again.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene, not checked against a translation this session; a strong parallel, though Hector leaves for war rather than for wealth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Aristophanes’ speech, Hephaestus offers two lovers the chance to be welded into one, so that they need never be parted in life or in death, and Aristophanes says no lover would refuse.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s Aristophanes explains love as the desire of two halves never to be separated again.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wants what Hephaestus offers: a union where the parting simply never happens.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; a strong expression of the wish never to part, though mythic and comic in tone.

kurals.tamil:
பிரிவுரைக்கும் வன்கண்ணர் ஆயின் அரிதவர்
நல்குவர் என்னும் நசை.
kurals.transliteration:
Pirivuraikkum vankannar aayin aridhavar
nalkuvar ennum nasai.
kurals.meaning: If he is hard-hearted enough to tell me to my face that he is leaving, then my hope that he will come back and be kind to me is a hope I can hardly keep.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a friend who can say ‘I’m going, bye!’ without looking sad at all. You might think, ‘If leaving me is that easy for them, will they really hurry back?’ The wife in this couplet thinks the same about her husband.
kurals.university: Pirivu uraikkum (பிரிவு உரைக்கும்) is ‘who speaks of parting’ and vaṉkaṇṇar (வன்கண்ணர்) ‘the hard-eyed, the cruel’: the very fact that he can announce the separation shows a hardness she did not expect. Nalkuvar (நல்குவர்) is ‘he will show grace or love’ and nacai (நசை) ‘longing hope’, which is arito, ‘hard to hold’ or, as most commentators read it, futile. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses vaṉkaṇ as ‘a heart of stone’ and Kalaignar calls the hope ‘vain’; Solomon Pappaiah adds that the parting is for work. Pope: ‘To cherish longing hope that he should ever gracious be, / Is hard, when he could stand, and of departure speak to me.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Uddhava brings Krishna’s message from Mathura, the gopis, addressing a bee as if it were Krishna’s messenger, complain that he who once loved them has left them and doubt that he will ever come back to them.
hinduism.explanation: In the ‘Bee Song’ the gopis voice hurt and bitterness at a beloved who was able to leave and stay away.
hinduism.tie_back: Their doubt is the Kural’s: one who could leave so easily is unlikely to return with tenderness.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; close in mood, though the devotional reading treats the separation as deepening love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But because I have said these things unto you, sorrow hath filled your heart.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus notes that his disciples are filled with grief simply because he has told them he is going away.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, it is the spoken announcement of departure that wounds.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; matches the pain of hearing the departure spoken, but Jesus promises to return, so the despair of the Kural is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “O my sons, go and find out about Joseph and his brother and despair not of relief from Allah. Indeed, no one despairs of relief from Allah except the disbelieving people.”
islam.explanation: Even after years of separation from Joseph, Jacob refuses to give up hope of reunion.
islam.tie_back: The verse is a counterpoint: the Kural’s heroine concludes her hope is futile, while Jacob holds that hope must never be abandoned.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a contrast in attitude to hope during separation rather than a parallel.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick; But desire fulfilled is a tree of life.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that hope endlessly postponed wears down the heart, while longing fulfilled gives life.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees nothing ahead but hope deferred, and her heart is already sick with it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close fit for the pain of uncertain hope, though general rather than about love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From craving springs grief, from craving springs fear. For one who is wholly free from craving there is no grief; whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief and fear to craving (tanha), the hungry wanting that will not let go.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s nacai, her longing hope, is just such craving, and as the verse says, it brings her grief.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it names the source of her pain, but as general doctrine with nothing specific to a departing lover.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you have no intention of abandoning pleasure, and still long for undertakings and property, my long talk has been to no purpose. I go, king, farewell.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citra, having failed to persuade his former brother to renounce, announces his departure plainly and leaves.
jainism.tie_back: A plainly spoken farewell like Citra’s is what the Kural’s heroine dreads; one who can say ‘I go’ so firmly is unlikely to turn back.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a firm spoken farewell, but between former brothers and with no romantic content, so the fit is loose.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phyllis, queen of Thrace, writes to Demophoon, who left promising to return by an agreed time; the time has long passed, and she slowly realises that he does not mean to come back.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s Heroides, Phyllis’s hope fades as each day without his ship shows how easily he could leave her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She lives out the Kural’s conclusion that the hope of a departed lover’s kindness is hard to keep.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s situation, not checked against a translation this session; a close parallel of hope fading after a promised return.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines hope as an inconstant joy and fear as an inconstant sadness, both born of the image of a future thing whose outcome we doubt, and notes that there is no hope without fear and no fear without hope.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, hope and fear are two sides of the same uncertainty.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows this: her hope that he will be kind on his return is inseparable from her fear that he will not.
philosophy.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part III, Definitions of the Affects 12-13 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of definitions, not checked word for word this session; an analytic account of her state rather than a parallel story.

kurals.tamil:
துறைவன் துறந்தமை தூற்றாகொல் முன்கை
இறைஇறவா நின்ற வளை.
kurals.transliteration:
Thuraivan thurandhamai thootraakol munkai
iraiiravaa nindra valai.
kurals.meaning: The bangles slipping down past the joint of my forearm, now that I have grown thin, will surely announce to the whole town that the lord of the seashore has left me.
kurals.elementary: When you are very sad, people can often tell even if you say nothing: your face looks different and you don’t feel like eating. In this couplet the wife has grown so thin with sadness that her bangles slide down her arm, and everyone who sees them knows her husband has gone away.
kurals.university: Tuṟaivaṉ (துறைவன்) is ‘lord of the shore’, the hero of the neytal (seashore) landscape, and tuṟantamai (துறந்தமை) ‘his having left’; tūṟṟākol (தூற்றாகொல்) asks ‘will they not proclaim (it abroad)?’, from tūṟṟu, ‘to spread gossip, publicise’. Muṉkai iṟai iṟavā niṉṟa vaḷai (முன்கை இறை இறவா நின்ற வளை) describes bangles ‘passing beyond the wrist-joint of the forearm’ because her arm has wasted, the standard Sangam sign of a woman pining in separation. Most commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Kalaignar) read the bangles as announcing his departure to the town; Solomon Pappaiah reads them as telling the heroine herself that he plans to leave, and Pope’s ‘announced before’ follows that anticipatory sense. Pope: ‘The bracelet slipping from my wrist announced before / Departure of the Prince that rules the ocean shore.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the opening of Kalidasa’s Meghaduta, the exiled yaksha, separated from his wife, has grown so thin that his golden bracelet has slipped from his forearm.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa uses the slipping bracelet as the visible mark of a lover wasting away in separation.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the same sign as the Kural’s slipping bangles, a body that publicly announces the absence of the beloved.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous image, not checked against a translation this session; a near one-to-one match of the slipping-bracelet sign, though here it is the man who wastes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes a sorrow so great that it shows in the body, in exhaustion and endless tears.
christianity.tie_back: As with the Kural’s bangles, grief that is not spoken still becomes visible in the body.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; shares the bodily signs of grief, but the psalm’s distress is not about a lover’s absence.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: Jacob tries to hold his grief for Joseph inside, but it shows in his body as his eyes whiten with sorrow.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s bangles, Jacob’s eyes show to everyone a grief of separation he did not proclaim himself.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (footnote markers removed); a strong match of hidden grief made visible in the body, though for a son rather than a husband.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Michal is taken from her husband Paltiel to be returned to David, Paltiel follows her, weeping as he goes, all the way to Bahurim, until he is ordered to go back.
judaism.explanation: The book of Samuel records a husband’s grief so open that he weeps along the road in front of everyone.
judaism.tie_back: Paltiel’s public tears, like the Kural’s slipping bangles, announce a separation to everyone who sees.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a brief narrative, not checked against JPS this session; a visible grief of separation, though the roles of the sexes are reversed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Patacara, having lost her husband, children and parents in a single disaster, wanders in grief so deep that her garment slips from her body without her noticing, and people call her Patacara because of it, until she meets the Buddha.
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada commentary tells how her grief became visible to everyone before she found peace in the Dhamma.
buddhism.tie_back: As with the Kural’s bangles, her outward state announces a loss she cannot hide.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 113, story of Patacara (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known commentarial story; the visible grief matches, but her loss is bereavement, a far heavier matter than a husband’s journey.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Firm and decided she cut off her tresses which were black like bees and dressed with a brush and comb.”
jainism.explanation: Forsaken by Arishtanemi, Rajimati gives up her beauty and cuts off her carefully dressed hair as she enters the order.
jainism.tie_back: Her shorn hair, like the Kural’s slipping bangles, is an outward sign everyone can see that her bridegroom has gone.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a visible sign following a beloved’s departure, but chosen deliberately as renunciation rather than suffered as wasting.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Hippolytus, the chorus and the nurse notice that Queen Phaedra has kept to her bed and refused food for days, wasting away, and they try to discover the hidden love that is the cause.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phaedra’s body gives away a love she is determined to keep secret.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As with the Kural’s slipping bangles, a lover’s wasting body makes public what she has not said.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known play; shares the theme of wasting that reveals love, but Phaedra’s love is forbidden, not the grief of a wife left behind.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Robert Burton lists the bodily symptoms of love-melancholy, including leanness, paleness, loss of appetite and sleeplessness, by which, he says, lovers are easily recognised by others.
philosophy.explanation: The Anatomy of Melancholy treats unhappy love as a condition with visible signs.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s slipping bangles are one such sign: the lover’s thinness gives her away to the whole town.
philosophy.source: Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy, Part 3, Section 2 (symptoms of love-melancholy) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the general content of the section, not checked word for word this session; a good thematic fit on bodily signs of love-sorrow.

kurals.tamil:
இன்னாது இனன்இல்ஊர் வாழ்தல் அதனினும்
இன்னாது இனியார்ப் பிரிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Innaadhu inanil oor vaazhdhal adhaninum
innaadhu iniyaarp pirivu.
kurals.meaning: It is painful to live in a town where no one is close to you; it is more painful still to be parted from the one you love.
kurals.elementary: Being the new kid in a school where you don’t know anyone feels lonely. But being far away from the person you love most feels even lonelier, even if you are surrounded by people. That is what this couplet says.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a graded comparison: iṉṉātu (இன்னாது, ‘painful’) is repeated, first for living in an iṉaṉ il ūr (இனன் இல் ஊர்), ‘a town without one’s own kind or kin’, and then, with ataṉiṉum (அதனினும், ‘more than that’), for iṉiyār pirivu (இனியார்ப் பிரிவு), ‘separation from the sweet one’. Iṉam can mean kin, friends of one’s own sort, or (for the heroine) companions such as the confidante, which Puliyur Kesikan specifies; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as ‘those who love us as our own’. The repetition of iṉṉātu echoes the device of the Iṉṉā Nāṟpatu, a didactic work among the Eighteen Minor Classics. Pope: ‘’Tis sad to sojourn in the town where no kind kinsmen dwell; / ’Tis sadder still to bid a friend beloved farewell.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: Separated from Sita, Rama wanders the shores of Lake Pampa in spring, and the beauty of the season, which would delight others, only deepens his grief for her.
hinduism.explanation: In the Kishkindha Kanda, even a beautiful place feels desolate to Rama without his wife.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama’s lament shows the Kural’s ranking: separation from the beloved makes any place more painful than mere loneliness would.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 1 (Rama’s lament at Pampa) (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known lament, not checked against a translation this session; a good thematic fit, though the comparison with a friendless town is implied rather than stated.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But we, brethren, being taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart, endeavoured the more abundantly to see your face with great desire.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Thessalonians that his separation from them, though brief and only in body, has made his longing to see them stronger.
christianity.tie_back: Paul, like the Kural, finds being parted from those dear to him one of the keenest pains, however short.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; captures the pain of separation from loved ones but not the comparison with living among strangers.

islam.quote_or_event: “Hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains, / Lamenting its banishment from its home.”
islam.explanation: Rumi opens the Masnavi with the reed cut from its reed-bed, whose music is a lament for its lost origin, a symbol of the soul separated from the Beloved.
islam.tie_back: The reed’s exile is the Kural’s ‘town without one’s own’, and its deeper grief is for the Beloved it was parted from.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, Prologue (tr. E.H. Whinfield)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Whinfield’s abridged translation); a strong match for exile and separation, read mystically rather than romantically.

judaism.quote_or_event: “How shall we sing the LORD’S song In a foreign land?”
judaism.explanation: The exiles in Babylon cannot bring themselves to sing, because they are cut off from Zion, the place they love.
judaism.tie_back: The psalm joins both pains the Kural compares: living in a foreign place, and being cut off from what one loves most.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); exile and separation from the beloved place, but national and religious rather than romantic.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names two pains: being with those we do not love, and being without those we do.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks the same two pains and finds the second, absence of the beloved, the worse.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a close structural parallel of two pains, though the Dhammapada advises non-attachment and does not rank them.

jainism.quote_or_event: “And we were gods having great power, in the regions of the gods. This is our sixth birth, in which we are separated from each other.”
jainism.explanation: King Brahmadatta recalls five past lives spent together with his brother Citra and grieves that in this sixth life they have been parted.
jainism.tie_back: After every hardship they shared together, it is separation that Brahmadatta names as the sorrow of this life, as the Kural ranks it above all else.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a genuine lament over separation from a beloved companion, though between brothers across rebirths.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On Calypso’s island, where a goddess loves him and offers him immortality, Odysseus spends his days sitting on the shore weeping, longing for home and for Penelope.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows that no comfort can make up for being parted from one’s own.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus lives the Kural’s comparison: a strange place is hard, but being parted from the beloved is harder still.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene, not checked against a translation this session; a strong parallel of exile and longing for a spouse.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero’s Laelius says that life without friendship is hardly worth living, and that nothing in nature is so opposed to solitude as human beings.
philosophy.explanation: On Friendship argues that human beings are made for companionship, and that being cut off from those we love takes the savour out of life.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero supports the Kural’s first claim about friendless places, and the Kural adds that losing the one dearest is worse still.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the dialogue’s general argument, not checked against a translation this session; it supports the first half of the Kural only.

kurals.tamil:
தொடிற்சுடின் அல்லது காமநோய் போல
விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ.
kurals.transliteration:
Thotirsudin alladhu kaamanoi pola
vitirsudal aatrumo thee.
kurals.meaning: Fire burns only when you touch it; can fire, like the sickness of love, burn you even when you move away from it?
kurals.elementary: A campfire only hurts if you touch it; step back and you are safe. But missing someone you love is a strange kind of fire: it hurts more the farther away they are. This couplet points out how odd and how painful that is.
kurals.university: The couplet is a vētṟumai (contrast) built on fire: toṭiṉ cuṭiṉ allatu (தொடின் சுடின் அல்லது), ‘other than burning when touched’, set against viṭiṉ cuṭal (விடின் சுடல்), ‘burning when let go of, when apart’. Kāmanōy (காமநோய்), ‘love-sickness’, is the subject that has this power, and āṟṟumō (ஆற்றுமோ), ‘is it able?’, makes it a rhetorical question to which the answer is no. Commentators agree on the reading; Kalaignar expands it to the lovers neither seeing nor touching each other, and Solomon Pappaiah renders it simply. The image is one of the most quoted in the Kāmattuppāl. Pope: ‘Fire burns the hands that touch; but smart of love / Will burn in hearts that far away remove.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Radha, separated from Krishna, feels sandal paste, cool breezes and moonlight, normally soothing, as burning fire, and her friend reports to Krishna that she is wasting in the heat of separation.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita Govinda uses the classical viraha theme, in which everything cool burns the separated lover.
hinduism.tie_back: Radha experiences the paradox of the Kural: in separation, love burns from a distance, and even cooling things become fire.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, cantos on Radha’s viraha (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known theme of the poem, not checked against a translation or tied to a specific verse this session; a strong thematic match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs describes love as a fire of the fiercest kind.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s love-sickness is just such a fire, so fierce that it burns even at a distance.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; shares the image of love as fire, without the specific paradox of burning at a distance.

islam.quote_or_event: “This plaint of the flute is fire, not mere air. / Let him who lacks this fire be accounted dead!”
islam.explanation: Rumi says the reed’s lament for its lost home is made of the fire of love, a fire every true lover carries.
islam.tie_back: The reed burns because it is separated, which is exactly the Kural’s fire that burns at a distance.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, Prologue (tr. E.H. Whinfield)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Whinfield); a close match of love’s fire kindled by separation, read mystically.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs says love’s fire cannot be put out by any amount of water.
judaism.tie_back: If love cannot be quenched by floods, it certainly cannot be quenched by distance, which is why it burns the Kural’s heroine from afar.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); love’s unquenchable fire fits, though distance is not mentioned.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no fire like lust; there is no grip like hatred; there is no net like delusion; there is no river like craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha ranks passion as the greatest of fires.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural agrees that love’s fire surpasses real fire; the Dhammapada sees this as reason to put it out.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the comparison of passion with fire is very close, though the Buddhist verdict is negative.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami, having renounced his kingdom, is untouched when told his city is burning, because he no longer claims anything as his own.
jainism.tie_back: Nami is the reverse of the Kural’s lover: through non-attachment, fire cannot burn him even up close, while love burns her even from afar.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a deliberate contrast on fire and attachment rather than a parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho describes the symptoms of love at the sight of the beloved: her tongue breaks, a thin fire runs beneath her skin, her eyes see nothing, her ears hum, and she feels close to death.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho’s poem is the classical description of love as a fire felt through the whole body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Sappho’s fire burns at the sight of the beloved; the Kural adds that it burns even more in her absence.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous poem, not checked against a translation this session; love as fire fits, but Sappho’s fire is kindled by presence, not absence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato’s Socrates describes the lover’s soul when separated from the beloved: the passages through which the wings grow dry up and close, and the soul is stung and goaded in agony until the sight of the beloved brings relief.
philosophy.explanation: In the Phaedrus, the absence of the beloved is a painful, burning torment, and his presence is the only cure.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato gives the Kural’s paradox a full account: love wounds most when the beloved is away.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; a strong conceptual match for pain that grows in absence.

kurals.tamil:
அரிதாற்றி அல்லல்நோய் நீக்கிப் பிரிவாற்றிப்
பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aridhaatri allalnoi neekkip pirivaatrip
pinirundhu vaazhvaar palar.
kurals.meaning: Many people, it seems, can agree to what should be impossible, drive away the pain of it, bear the separation, and still go on living afterwards.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes a grown-up says, ‘Lots of people manage when someone they love goes away,’ and you think, ‘Maybe they do, but I don’t know how I would!’ The wife in this couplet says something like that: other people may be able to bear it, but she is not sure she can.
kurals.university: The couplet strings together four participles: aritu āṟṟi (அரிது ஆற்றி), ‘bearing what is hard’ or consenting to the impossible; allal nōy nīkki (அல்லல் நோய் நீக்கி), ‘driving off the sickness of sorrow’; pirivu āṟṟi (பிரிவு ஆற்றி), ‘enduring the separation’; and piṉ iruntu vāḻvār (பின் இருந்து வாழ்வார்), ‘those who live on afterwards’, before the predicate palar (பலர்), ‘are many’. Commentators differ on the tone: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as a straightforward observation that many women endure, Solomon Pappaiah as a statement about wives whose husbands go to earn, while Kalaignar and Pope’s prose gloss (‘As if there were many indeed…’) take it as irony, so that the heroine implies she is not one of them. The chapter title, Pirivāṟṟāmai, ‘not being able to bear separation’, supports the ironic reading. Pope’s verse: ‘Sorrow’s sadness meek sustaining, Driving sore distress away, / Separation uncomplaining Many bear the livelong day!’

hinduism.quote_or_event: Held captive in Ravana’s Ashoka grove for many months, Sita endures separation from Rama, refusing every pressure and keeping herself alive by her hope in him.
hinduism.explanation: The Sundara Kanda presents Sita as the model of a wife who bears an almost unbearable separation and survives it.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita is one of the ‘many’ the Kural speaks of, who endure the impossible and live on.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known narrative; it fits the literal reading of endurance, while the Kural’s probable irony is not reflected.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to endure hardship patiently, sustained by hope.
christianity.tie_back: Paul describes the patient endurance that the Kural says many manage, and that its heroine doubts she can.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a general call to endurance, with no reference to love or separation.

islam.quote_or_event: “Rather, your souls have enticed you to something, so patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them to me all together.”
islam.explanation: Having now lost two sons, Jacob chooses beautiful patience and lives on in hope of reunion.
islam.tie_back: Jacob is one of the many who bear separation and keep living, the very thing the Kural’s heroine says others manage.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a good match for enduring separation, though between father and sons.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells how Rachel, daughter of Kalba Savua, married Akiva and then sent him away to study Torah, enduring twelve years and then another twelve of separation in poverty until he returned as a great sage.
judaism.explanation: Rachel is honoured in rabbinic tradition for bearing a long separation for the sake of her husband’s learning.
judaism.tie_back: Rachel is a clear example of the ‘many’ who agree to a hard parting and live through it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known aggadah, not checked against the text this session; a close match for a wife who consents to and endures separation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “This is the greater: the tears you have shed while transmigrating & wandering this long, long time — crying & weeping from being joined with what is displeasing, being separated from what is pleasing — not the water in the four great oceans.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his monks that, across countless lives, every being has wept over separations more than all the oceans hold.
buddhism.tie_back: In the Buddhist view everyone has endured separation from what is dear countless times, which gives the Kural’s ‘many’ a cosmic scale.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 15.3, Assu Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a strong match on the universality of separation, used to argue for release rather than endurance.

jainism.quote_or_event: Forsaken by Arishtanemi on her wedding day, Rajimati does not die of grief but enters the order, leads many relatives and servants to follow her, and eventually attains omniscience and final liberation.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana shows Rajimati enduring her abandonment and turning it into a spiritual life.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati is one of the ‘many’ who bear separation and live on, though the Jain path transforms the grief rather than simply enduring it.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a narrative read on sacred-texts.com this session; a fit for the literal reading of endurance, though its resolution is renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope waits twenty years for Odysseus, putting off her suitors by weaving and unweaving Laertes’ shroud, grieving for him constantly yet keeping the household going until he returns.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer presents Penelope as the classic example of a wife who endures a long separation.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope is one of the ‘many’ the Kural speaks of, who bear the pain of absence and live on.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous story; a clear example of endurance, while the Kural’s probable irony is not reflected.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Writing to Lucilius on the death of a friend, Seneca allows that tears may fall but urges that grief be moderate, noting that time eventually ends grief even for those who will not end it themselves.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca treats the endurance of loss as something reason and time make possible for most people.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca speaks for the ‘many’ who recover from separation; the Kural’s heroine doubts she will be among them.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the letter’s argument, not checked against a translation this session; it concerns death rather than a journey, so the fit is partial.
